explicit_validation.explanation: The paper explicitly validates FQ-Score (which includes LLM-as-a-judge components) against human evaluation through two clinician reader studies, reporting quantitative correlations and agreement metrics

prompts.notes: Prompts for LLM evaluation are mentioned as being available in Appendix A.5 but not shown in the provided text

human_eval_details.num_evaluators: 5 in first study, 2 in second study

inter_annotator_agreement.value: First study: 0.406 (95% CI: 0.21 to 0.65); Second study: 0.539 (95% CI: 0.16 to 0.78)
inter_annotator_agreement.interpretation: First study: considerable variability; Second study: moderate to substantial reliability

guidelines.notes: Guidelines adapted from prior clinical NLP works; clinicians evaluated factual correctness per step (yes/no), relevance/usefulness per step (0-10), overall logical consistency (0-10)

sample_size.validated_by_both: First study: 20 ToQ samples; Second study: CoT, CoQ, and ToQ outputs (exact size unspecified but based on same 20 samples)
sample_size.notes: Two reader studies with clinicians on MedQA samples

quantitative_scores.notes: First reader study - FQ-Score vs clinician mean opinion scores

correlation_interpretation.threshold_used: Not explicitly stated, but r=0.866 is described as 'strong correlation'

validation_results.summary_finding: FQ-Score shows strong correlation (r=0.866) with clinician judgments, with ToQ achieving the highest alignment (ρ=0.990, p=0.001) among all prompting methods evaluated.

criteria_mapping.notes: LLM evaluates additional technical metrics while human focuses on clinical judgment aspects, but both evaluate core quality dimensions
